column1: What does the Atomicity property guarantee in database transactions?
column2: It guarantees that a transaction executes in an all-or-nothing manner, where either all operations complete or none take effect.

column1: What is the primary objective of the Consistency property in an RDBMS transaction?
column2: It ensures that a transaction transitions the database from one valid state to another valid state.

column1: How does the Isolation property affect concurrently executing database transactions?
column2: It ensures concurrent transactions execute independently without exposing intermediate, uncommitted state to each other.

column1: What does the Durability property guarantee once a transaction commits?
column2: It guarantees that committed changes persist permanently in the database, even in the event of a system failure.

column1: Which lock type must a transaction acquire before reading a data item?
column2: A transaction must acquire a readlock on the data item prior to reading it.

column1: Which lock type is required before a transaction can execute a write operation on a data item?
column2: A transaction must acquire a writelock on the data item prior to writing.

column1: Under what condition do two lock requests on the same variable NOT conflict with each other?
column2: Two lock requests do not conflict when both transactions request a readlock on the variable.

column1: What occurs when a transaction requests a writelock on a data item currently held under a readlock by another transaction?
column2: A lock conflict occurs, requiring the requesting transaction to either wait or roll back.

column1: What is a lock upgrade in database concurrency control?
column2: It is the conversion of an existing readlock held by a transaction into a writelock on the same variable.

column1: What permission restriction characterizes the growing phase of Two-Phase Locking (2PL)?
column2: The transaction can acquire new locks, but it is strictly forbidden from releasing any locks.

column1: What restriction applies to a transaction during the shrinking phase of Two-Phase Locking (2PL)?
column2: The transaction can release existing locks, but it cannot acquire any new locks.

column1: What defines a database deadlock during concurrent transaction processing?
column2: A state where two or more transactions are blocked indefinitely, each waiting for a lock held by the other.

column1: How is a deadlock identified in a transaction precedence dependency graph?
column2: A deadlock is indicated by the existence of a cycle in the precedence graph.

column1: How does a database system resolve an active deadlock once it is detected?
column2: The system aborts and rolls back one of the involved transactions to release its held locks.

column1: What causes a cascading rollback in database concurrency control?
column2: It occurs when rolling back one transaction forces other transactions that read its uncommitted updates to also roll back.

column1: What are the two primary strategic options for a transaction encountering a lock conflict?
column2: The transaction can either wait for the lock to be released or abort and roll back.

column1: What primary operational purpose does the Two-Phase Locking (2PL) protocol fulfill?
column2: It prevents shared data corruption by ensuring serializable execution among concurrent transactions.

column1: In relational database terminology, what is a table called?
column2: A relation.

column1: What is the Big O cost of finding any ONE student in a class of $n$ students?
column2: $O(1)$: constant time regardless of $n$.

column1: What are the best-case, worst-case and average-case costs of a linear search for one name in a list?
column2: Best $O(1)$, worst $O(n)$, average $O(n)$ (half the list on average).

column1: What does $\lg n$ denote in the lecture's Big O notation?
column2: The binary logarithm (base 2); $\log$ alone denotes base 10.

column1: In a B tree search, how do we know a value does not exist?
column2: The search reaches the leaf level without finding it.

column1: In a B+ tree, what is the rule for values relative to a separator?
column2: Values on the left are smaller; values on the right are larger than or equal to the separator.

column1: Must a separator value in a B+ tree non-leaf node exist in the database?
column2: No. A separator only guides the search, so a value like 20 can be a separator even if no record has 20.

column1: In a B+ tree range query, when does the scan of sibling leaves stop?
column2: When the next sibling's smallest value already exceeds the upper bound of the range.

column1: What is the update cost of a B / B+ tree index?
column2: $O(\lg n)$, the same order as its search cost.

column1: What does it mean that a B / B+ tree is balanced?
column2: The path length from the root to every leaf node is the same.

column1: Can one table have more than one index?
column2: Yes. A table can have multiple indices, e.g., one on module code and one on grade.

column1: Why is the space overhead of an index smaller than the records themselves?
column2: The index stores only pointers to records; there is always only one copy of the record contents.

column1: How does an RDBMS query optimizer choose a query plan?
column2: It keeps statistics about the database (e.g., number of records) and automatically picks the estimated best plan.

column1: What are the two main challenges in handling database transactions?
column2: Concurrency control (many users on the same data) and recovery (restoring contents after failure).

column1: Why does an ATM wait for an "OK" acknowledgement from the central database after an update?
column2: The network may drop a message; if no OK arrives in time, the ATM resends the message.

column1: What defines a correct concurrent execution of transactions?
column2: One equivalent to a serial execution, where transactions run one by one; any serial order is deemed correct.

column1: Name two concurrency control methods other than two-phase locking.
column2: Timestamp ordering and Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC).

column1: Does a transaction holding a writelock on $x$ also need a readlock on $x$?
column2: No. A writelock is an upgraded readlock, so it also permits reading.

column1: What is the core principle of log-based recovery?
column2: Save to the log before writing to the database system.

column1: What three kinds of entries must a recovery log contain?
column2: A record of each transaction's start, a record of its commit, and the update contents.

column1: How does a blocking checkpoint work?
column2: All database updates are stopped, a snapshot is taken, and recovery only scans back to the closest checkpoint.

column1: Besides a snapshot, what does a fuzzy checkpoint record?
column2: The list of transactions that are running at the time of the checkpoint.

column1: What is the worst-case recovery cost with fuzzy checkpoints?
column2: $O(n)$: scanning backwards to the first log entry, which only happens with a very short log or an unreasonably long transaction.
